vignette:
# The Weight of Numbers

Rohan is a 36-year-old South Asian man who works as a senior accountant at a mid-sized firm in the city. He sits across from his therapist with his hands folded neatly in his lap, his posture careful and controlled — the kind of stillness that looks less like calm and more like a man who has spent decades practicing how not to take up too much space.

He grew up in a household where the walls were thin and the nights were loud. From the time he was about six years old until he left for university at eighteen, Rohan watched his father hurt his mother. Not every night, but often enough that every night felt like a possibility. He remembers lying in bed listening for the particular sound of his father's key in the door — whether it turned slowly or quickly, whether there were footsteps or silence after — and making calculations in his head about what the evening would bring. He learned to read the atmosphere of a room the way other children learned to read books. He became very good at it.

His mother never left. She called it family. She called it izzat — honor. Rohan called it nothing, because there were no words for it in his house, and so he carried it without language for thirty years.

He married in his late twenties, a woman his family approved of, and for a brief time he believed he had outrun the past. But he was hypervigilant in ways he could not explain to her — checking that doors were locked, flinching at raised voices in restaurants, going cold and unreachable after minor disagreements. She said he was emotionally absent. She was not wrong. They divorced after four years. He does not blame her.

Now he lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment that he keeps immaculately organized. His work, in many ways, is the one place he feels genuinely competent and safe. Numbers follow rules. Spreadsheets do not escalate. He is meticulous, well-regarded, and has been passed over for a management role twice because, his supervisor noted gently, he struggles to delegate and becomes visibly tense in team meetings when voices rise even slightly during debate.

The past several months have been harder. A colleague going through a divorce began talking openly in the office about arguments with his wife, and something in Rohan shifted. He started sleeping poorly again — waking at two or three in the morning with his heart already racing, certain something is wrong, lying rigid in the dark until his body slowly accepts that he is safe. He has dreams he cannot always remember but wakes from with his jaw aching from clenching. During the day, he finds himself scanning rooms when he enters them, noting exits, watching the body language of the men around him. He has stopped going to his parents' home for Sunday dinners, telling himself it is because of work, though he knows it is because sitting at that table, in that kitchen, with his father now old and quiet, makes him feel six years old again and completely without protection.

He describes his emotional life as "flat, mostly," punctuated by moments of anger that frighten him with their intensity — not because he acts on them, but because he recognizes something of his father in the heat of them, and that recognition is its own kind of terror. He is careful never to raise his voice. He is careful in almost every way imaginable.

What brought him to therapy, finally, was a moment three months ago when a neighbor's argument bled through the apartment wall late at night, and Rohan found himself on the floor of his hallway, back against the wall, knees to his chest, waiting for something to happen. He sat there for two hours. In the morning, he made an appointment.

He says he is not sure what he is hoping for. He says he has never told anyone the full story before. He says this quietly, looking at his hands, and then he begins.
